quotes.quote: A challenging benchmark measuring language models' ability to extract, reason about, and synthesize information from long-form documents ranging from 10k to 100k tokens (measured using the cl100k_base tokenizer).
Kimi K3 (Max) scores the highest on AA-LCR v1.1 with a score of 88.7%, followed by Step 5 Preview with a score of 88.3% and Kimi K3.1 Pro with a score of 86.3%
27 of 596 models
Long-form text comprehension represents an under-studied class of evaluations where humans dramatically outscore language models, despite expanding context windows in current AI systems.

Each question demands multi-step reasoning to synthesize information from dispersed sections, understand complex domain-specific content, and produce unambiguous answers that mid-2024 frontier models achieve less than 50% accuracy on.

quotes.cite: official-page@How is Artificial Analysis Long Context Reasoning scored?
quotes.quote: AA-LCR is scored with pass/fail grading on open-answer questions. A model receives credit when its answer is judged equivalent to the official answer by another LLM, and the final AA-LCR score is the model's average pass rate across the benchmark.

quotes.cite: official-page@Why is Artificial Analysis Long Context Reasoning important?
quotes.quote: AA-LCR is important because a large context window does not guarantee that a model can reason effectively over long documents.

quotes.quote: AA-LCR includes 100 hard text-based questions that require reasoning across multiple real-world documents, with each document set averaging ~100k input tokens. Questions are designed such that answers cannot be directly retrieved from documents and must instead be reasoned from multiple information sources.

Sixteen corrected answer keys. Each one was re-verified against the question's own source documents. Most were values stored as a decimal fraction where the question asked for a percentage (question 28, 0.658, is now 65.8%), or a date stored as a spreadsheet serial number (question 40, 45444, is now June 2024). Four were corrections to the answer itself rather than its notation: questions 10, 25, 30 and 67.
A judge system prompt. The equality checker previously ran with no system prompt, which left it to improvise on unit conversion, notation and multi-value answers one call at a time.
The questions and the document sets are unchanged. Scores measured on version 1.0.0 are not directly comparable with scores measured on version 1.1.

AA-LCR was created through a rigorous multi-phase process involving several members of the Artificial Analysis research team and more than a dozen undergraduate students who were engaged on a short-term contract basis to write and/or validate questions.

Document Curation: We selected diverse document sets (company reports, government consultations, legal documents, academic papers) averaging ~100,000 tokens each, representing real materials knowledge workers analyze.

Undergraduate students from various disciplines developed questions with access via a dataset development dashboard to non-frontier test models to validate question difficulty (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-70B, Gemini 1.5 Flash).
These models were specifically chosen to give creators a sense of AI capabilities without access to frontier models, preventing adversarial selection against particular frontier models.
Human performance revealed the benchmark's challenging nature - individual evaluators achieved modest accuracy rates, typically answering 40-60% of questions correctly on the first attempt
Questions failing verification were revised or discarded
Every question in AA-LCR was answered correctly by at least one human tester, ensuring all questions have verified solutions
AA-LCR comprises 100 questions across 7 types of text-only documents (i.e. Company Reports, Industry Reports, Government Consultations, Academia, Legal, Marketing Materials and Survey Reports).

We load the relevant documents for each question into context in the same prompt as the question text.
Answer the following question using the input documents provided above.
Reported token counts per question are based on the completed prompt, using the cl100k_base tokenizer from tiktoken.
The order in which documents are loaded in matters - they should be added to the prompt template in the order of the filenames in data_source_filenames.
We use an LLM-based equality checker to evaluate responses. The checker receives a system prompt and a user prompt.
Decide whether the CANDIDATE ANSWER is correct or incorrect against the OFFICIAL ANSWER.

Numbers should still match when they are the same value written differently, e.g., a percentage, a count of percentage points, and the equivalent decimal fraction are the same value: 0.675, "67.5%" and "67.5 percentage points" all match.
Grade the value the CANDIDATE ANSWER finally commits to, and it must commit to one.
GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) is used as the equality checker model.
